newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Heart pills prescribed for ailing Mir commander.
newsitem.headline: Heart pills prescribed for ailing Mir commander.

text.p: The Mission Control doctor advising the troubled space station Mir told the ship's commander on Tuesday to take sedatives and medicine to stabilise his heartbeat.
Mission doctor Igor Goncharov earlier said the head of the three-man crew, Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, had developed a heart condition with an irregular heartbeat that was a concern.
Tsibliyev has been under great strain since June 25 when an unmanned Progress cargo craft under his control collided with one of Mir's modules in the worst accident in its history.
The Russian press has said he was responsible for the accident, although space officials say they have not yet determined whether man or machine was at fault.
Goncharov sought to calm Tsibliyev during a radio link up between Mission Control outside Moscow and Mir on Tuesday.
"I repeat that we are assessing your work to be of the highest calibre," he said.

"Vassily, in terms of calming procedures, you'll take from the cabinet in the morning at 10 or 11 a tablet called Rudotel and at night 30 minutes before going to sleep one tablet of Tsenozipam," he said, referring to two sedative medicines.

"From cabinet SS-72 take one tablet of Etmozin four times a day every four hours for three days," he added in his long-distance diagnosis. Etmosin is an anti-arrhythmia which seeks to assure a normal heart beat.
Doctors said they would review the dosage and its results after three days. Mission Control also asked Tsibliyev to reduce his daily exercise routine.

"You have to limit the burden of your training sessions and do only 50 percent once a day," Goncharov said. "We'll be monitoring you and monitoring how you feel...because the pulse and blood pressure are concerning us and we must control these parameters."

Vital repairs to the Mir space station, which lost about half its power in the accident, may not take place for about 10 more days because of Tsibliyev's health problems, officials said on Tuesday. The repairs had been expected on Friday or Saturday.
